The security team flagged that our API returns stack traces in 500 errors. How urgent?

High priority. Stack traces expose class names, file paths, library versions, and internal API boundaries — useful to an attacker for targeting known CVEs. Fix: return a generic message with a correlation ID to the client, log the full trace server-side. This should be a blocker before the next production deployment.
We're evaluating Redis sorted sets vs a token bucket for per-user rate limiting at 1000 req/min.

Token bucket is the standard recommendation at user-level: two values per user, cheap in Redis, handles burst absorption naturally. If you cannot tolerate a 1000-req burst in the first second, cap the bucket at a fraction of the per-minute limit (e.g., 200 tokens max). Sliding window log is more accurate but expensive — one sorted-set entry per request plus GC overhead.
API response times increased 40ms after adding three indexed columns to a 180M-row table. What to check?

Check the slow query log for plan changes — new indexes may be selected for reads they are not optimal for. Check autovacuum activity; a migration on 180M rows can leave dead tuples that inflate bloat and slow sequential scans. Run ANALYZE manually if autovacuum has not caught up. Confirm the index creation used CONCURRENTLY.
The team is proposing a 99.95% SLA for the API gateway. We currently target 99.9%. How do I frame the gap?

99.9% allows ~8.7 h/year of downtime; 99.95% allows ~4.4 h. The question is whether halving the error budget is worth the engineering investment. For most gateways the gap shows in planned maintenance windows and MTTR on tail incidents. If your current MTTR is 45 min, you are likely already at 99.95% under normal conditions.
Onboarding docs are 18 months out of date. Full rewrite or incremental updates?

Incremental updates. A full rewrite takes longer than planned and leaves the stale docs in production during the rewrite, creating two sources of truth. Triage first: find which sections generate the most Slack questions and which are factually wrong vs merely incomplete. Update those first, then schedule quarterly reviews going forward.
The data team estimates 3 months for a greenfield feature store. Is that realistic?

Optimistic for a store that serves both training pipelines and real-time inference. The timeline is dominated by the offline/online consistency model, the historical backfill pipeline, and the API contract with existing teams. Scoped to offline training features only, 3 months is feasible. Real-time serving adds point-in-time correctness complexity and needs a separate phase.
The Q3 infrastructure budget shows compute at $420k, networking $85k, storage $110k. Does compute look right for the planned GPU cluster expansion?

The $420k compute allocation is tight for a GPU cluster expansion. A meaningful experiment typically needs 50-200 node-hours, at $10-18/hr for A100 nodes. Reserve at least 30% as contingency for re-runs. The $85k networking budget should cover inter-region egress for model weights, but confirm transfer costs before committing.
We're splitting the auth refactor across two sprints rather than one. Is that reasonable?

Two sprints is safer if sprint 1 ends in a deployable, backward-compatible state — new auth path behind a feature flag, old path still active. Sprint 2 migrates callers and removes the flag. This gives a rollback point if sprint 1 reveals unexpected session-handling dependencies.
Our CI pipeline has 47 jobs. Is migrating from Jenkins to GitHub Actions worth it?

At 47 jobs the migration is significant work. The largest cost is translating stateful jobs that rely on Jenkins plugins. Start with a parallel PoC on the 5-10 most-used jobs, measure wall-clock time and cost, then commit to full migration only if the savings justify it. Check that GPU or large-RAM jobs are covered by self-hosted runners before finalising the migration plan.
